summary: A notice from UCSB about changes to how network users log in to its On-line System. Since all network users shared one account, usage could not be tracked by site. From June 1, 1972, users supply their site name as the user name and their own name or NIC ID as the job name. A list of site designations is included.

eli5.summary: Everyone used the same name tag at a club, so the club could not tell who came. Now each visitor must write their own group name so the club can count.

questions: how to log in to ucsb on-line system
subtitle: New login requirements to track network user access and billing.

tldr.problem: UCSB offers free network access to its on-line system to all ARPANET sites, but all users share a single account (ARPA), making it impossible to track usage by site.
tldr.mechanism: UCSB changes the login procedure effective June 1, 1972: users must supply their site name as the user name and their own name (or NIC ID) as the job name, along with fixed user number and ID.
tldr.outcome: UCSB can now monitor usage by site and bill sites that choose production access instead of experimental access.

today: RFC 350 describes a policy change from May 1972 at UCSB for network access accounting. It is marked Unknown status. The RFC includes a comprehensive list of early ARPANET site abbreviations (AMES, BBN, MIT, CMU, Stanford, UCLA, RAND, etc.), documenting the network's early membership.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 350 announces a policy change at UCSB's Computer Research Lab for network access to the UCSB On-line System (based on the Culler-Fried System). For the past year, UCSB provided free experimental access to ARPANET sites. All users logged in with the same shared account (User Number 196, ID 57372, User Name ARPA).

Because all users shared one account, UCSB could not track which sites were using the system or measure usage. Connect time in April 1972 totaled 152 hours. To improve accounting and distinguish between experimental and production use, UCSB is changing the login procedure.
sections.eli5: A school shared its computer with everyone on the network for free. Everyone used the same login name, so nobody knew which school was using it or how much. This made accounting impossible.

sections.title: New Login Procedure
sections.content:
Effective June 1, 1972, the new login parameters are:

  • User Number: 196 (unchanged)
  • ID: 57372 (unchanged)
  • User Name: [site designation] (e.g., BBN, MIT, RAND)
  • Job Name: [your name] or [your NIC ID]

Each ARPANET site has a two or three letter site designation listed at the end of RFC 350 (AMES, BBN, MIT, RAND, UCLA, etc.). Using the site name as the user name lets UCSB track usage by organization.
sections.eli5: Now you type your school's name where it says user, and your own name where it says job. UCSB can then see which school is logging in.

sections.title: Access Levels
sections.content:
UCSB reminds network users that free accounts are for network experimentation and casual use only, so people can learn the Culler-Fried System. Sites planning production work must open a private paid account with UCSB's Computer Center and pay for the computer time used.

UCSB also continues to offer limited free remote batch support for sites debugging network software, with the same constraint: production batch jobs require a paid account.
sections.eli5: The free account is for trying things out and learning. If you want to run real work, you have to open a paid account.
